title: Characters Under Glass
theme: Literary analysis: complex characters and turning points
objectives: I can use ten literary terms and character words to describe how a character thinks, acts, and changes.
I can explain what makes a character dynamic and point to the turning point in a story.
I can tell an antagonist from a villain and explain what an epiphany does in a plot.
I can write a short character analysis using at least four words from this unit and evidence from a text.
rationale: Advanced character analysis needs two kinds of words. The first kind names a character's role or change in the plot (antagonist, dynamic, epiphany, redemption). The second kind describes a flawed or contradictory person precisely (pragmatic, idealistic, volatile, enigmatic, disillusioned, ruthless). Together they let students replace vague words such as mean, nice, or weird with claims they can support from a text. The passage is a student's analysis of an invented novel, so students see the words used as evidence-based claims and not as labels. The unit builds on irony, foils and personas from earlier units.

words.def: The character or force that opposes the main character in a story.
words.ex: In many fairy tales, the wicked stepmother is the antagonist who stands in the heroine's way.
words.ex2: The antagonist of the sea novel is not a person but the storm itself.
words.nonExample: A helpful friend who supports the main character is an ally, not an antagonist.

apps.academic: Literary analysis asks what the antagonist wants and why it conflicts with the main character's goal.
apps.spoken: Who is the antagonist in that movie?
apps.writing: Define the antagonist by opposition to the main character's goal, not by whether the character is evil.

cloze.s: The detective's greatest obstacle was the cunning ___, a thief who always seemed to be one step ahead.

cloze2.s: In the survival story, the harsh desert is the ___, working against every step the hikers take.

misuse.s: The antagonist was the hero's best friend, who cheered for every success and helped with every difficulty.
misuse.why: An antagonist opposes the main character; a friend who helps at every step is an ally.

visual.alt: A theater mask beside crossed swords.

words.def: A sudden moment of understanding when something becomes clear.
words.ex: While washing dishes, she had an epiphany about how to end her story.
words.ex2: In the novel, the narrator's epiphany comes when he sees his own reflection in a puddle and understands what he has become.
words.nonExample: A slow change of opinion over many months is not an epiphany.

apps.academic: In a story, an epiphany often marks the moment a character sees the truth about a situation or about themselves.
apps.spoken: I had an epiphany: the answer was in the question all along.
apps.writing: Show an epiphany by describing the moment and then showing what the character does next.

cloze.s: After weeks of confusion, Dana had an ___ in the shower and finally understood how the poem's two halves fit together.

cloze2.s: The scientist's ___ came suddenly: the strange result was caused by the temperature of the room.

misuse.s: Her epiphany was a slow, gradual change of opinion that took place over ten years.
misuse.why: An epiphany is a sudden understanding; a change that takes ten years is gradual.

visual.alt: A glowing light bulb with sparks around it.

words.def: Changing in important ways over time; used for a character who grows or changes during a story.

senses.example: The dynamic speaker kept the whole audience on the edge of their seats.

words.ex: Scrooge is a dynamic character, because he begins as a miser and ends as a generous man.
words.ex2: In a dynamic story, the main character's beliefs at the end are not the same as at the beginning.
words.nonExample: A character who has the same habits and beliefs on the last page as on the first is static, not dynamic.

apps.academic: A dynamic character is changed by conflict, so ask what event causes the change.
apps.spoken: That character is dynamic: look how different she is by the end.
apps.writing: Support the claim that a character is dynamic with two quotations, one from early and one from late in the story.

cloze.s: Because Marcus begins the novel selfish and ends it generous, he is a ___ character.

cloze2.s: Teachers often ask students to prove that a main character is ___ by comparing his choices in the first and final chapters.

misuse.s: A dynamic character stays exactly the same from the first page to the last.
misuse.why: A dynamic character changes; a character who stays exactly the same is static.

visual.alt: A character at the start of a story, then an event, then a changed character at the end.

words.frame: A dynamic character I know is ___, who changes from ___ to ___.

words.def: Dealing with problems in a practical, realistic way rather than by ideals or theories.
words.ex: The pragmatic mayor chose the cheaper bridge design because it could be finished before winter.
words.ex2: A pragmatic solution to the crowded hallway is to stagger the dismissal times.
words.nonExample: Waiting for a perfect plan that can never be built is not pragmatic.

apps.academic: A pragmatic character focuses on what works rather than on what is perfect.
apps.spoken: Let's be pragmatic: we have one hour and two tasks.
apps.writing: Pragmatic describes a way of solving problems; it shows a character's priorities and is not always an insult.

cloze.s: The ___ coach said that winning the next game mattered more than playing a beautiful style.

cloze2.s: Instead of arguing about whose idea was best, Lena took the ___ approach and tried the fastest one first.

misuse.s: The pragmatic engineer rejected every practical option and insisted on a plan that could never be built.
misuse.why: Pragmatic means practical and realistic; insisting on an impossible plan is the opposite.

visual.alt: A wrench beside a check mark.

words.def: Guided by high hopes about how things should be, even when those hopes are hard to reach.
words.ex: The idealistic young teacher believed that every student could learn to love reading.
words.ex2: She was an idealistic volunteer who thought one weekend of cleanup would solve the town's pollution.
words.nonExample: A person who expects every plan to fail because people are selfish is not idealistic.

apps.academic: In stories, idealistic characters are often tested when their beliefs collide with reality.
apps.spoken: I know I am being idealistic, but I think we can fix this.
apps.writing: Idealistic can be praise or criticism, so show which by what happens to the character's hopes.

cloze.s: The ___ candidate promised to end every problem in the city within a year, ignoring how hard that would be.

cloze2.s: As an ___ college student, he believed that one well-written letter could end a war.

misuse.s: The idealistic character had no hopes at all and laughed at anyone who believed in a better world.
misuse.why: Idealistic means guided by high hopes; laughing at a better world is cynical.

visual.alt: A bright star beside a white dove.

words.def: Likely to change suddenly and sharply, especially in mood or in a situation.

senses.example: Gasoline is a volatile liquid that evaporates easily.

words.ex: His volatile temper made the whole team nervous, because he could be cheerful at noon and furious by one.
words.ex2: The volatile weather flipped from sunshine to hail in an hour.
words.nonExample: A person who stays calm and even-tempered all day is not volatile.

apps.academic: A volatile character is unpredictable, which keeps readers unsure about what will happen next.
apps.spoken: The situation is volatile, so be careful what you say.
apps.writing: Use volatile for quick, unpredictable shifts, not for something that is merely loud.

cloze.s: The coach's ___ mood meant that no player knew whether a mistake would earn a joke or a lecture.

cloze2.s: Because the political situation was ___, the embassy warned travelers that conditions could change within hours.

misuse.s: The volatile river was perfectly calm and predictable, never changing in speed or mood.
misuse.why: Volatile means likely to change suddenly; a river that never changes is the opposite.

visual.alt: A volcano beside a bolt of lightning.

words.frame: A volatile temper can make people ___.

words.def: Mysterious and hard to understand or interpret.
words.ex: The enigmatic painter never explained her work, and critics argued for years about its meaning.
words.ex2: He gave an enigmatic smile that could have meant yes, no, or maybe.
words.nonExample: A plainly written instruction manual is not enigmatic.

apps.academic: Authors make a character enigmatic by withholding information about the character's past.
apps.spoken: She gave me an enigmatic look and walked away.
apps.writing: Show that a character is enigmatic through what other characters cannot explain about him.

cloze.s: The ___ stranger gave no name and answered every question with a riddle.

cloze2.s: The poem's ___ final line left readers debating what the poet really meant.

misuse.s: The enigmatic instructions were so clear and simple that everyone understood them at once.
misuse.why: Enigmatic means mysterious and hard to understand; clear, simple instructions are the opposite.

visual.alt: A question mark beside a pair of dark sunglasses.

words.frame: An enigmatic character is one whose ___ we cannot ___.

words.def: Disappointed after learning that something is not as good or as true as you believed.
words.ex: Disillusioned by years of broken promises, the voters stayed home.
words.ex2: She grew disillusioned with the club when she learned that its leaders had lied about the money.
words.nonExample: A person who is still excited and trusting after a promise is kept is not disillusioned.

apps.academic: Many novels about war follow a character who becomes disillusioned with ideals he once believed.
apps.spoken: I am disillusioned with that show after the last season.
apps.writing: Say what the character believed before: disillusioned always means a belief was lost.

cloze.s: The ___ young reporter quit after learning that her editor had been hiding the truth she believed the paper stood for.

cloze2.s: Voters grew ___ after many years of promises that were never kept.

misuse.s: He felt disillusioned when his hopes came true and everything turned out even better than he had imagined.
misuse.why: Disillusioned means disappointed that something is not as good as believed; things turning out better is the opposite.

visual.alt: A deflated balloon beside a broken heart.

words.def: Having or showing no pity or concern for others when trying to get what you want.
words.ex: The ruthless boss fired workers without warning to save money.
words.ex2: Her ruthless ambition led her to step over anyone who got in her way.
words.nonExample: A fair coach who gives every player a chance is not ruthless.

morph.note: Ruth is an old English word for pity that survives mainly in this word.

apps.academic: Authors make an antagonist ruthless by showing characters being harmed without regret.
apps.spoken: That plan was ruthless, but it worked.
apps.writing: Ruthless means lacking pity; add an example so readers see what the character actually does.

cloze.s: The ___ dictator crushed every protest and never showed mercy to prisoners.

cloze2.s: In the final race, the ___ rival pulled ahead by tripping the leader and pretending not to notice.

misuse.s: The ruthless judge wept with pity for every defendant and gave all of them the lightest possible sentence.
misuse.why: Ruthless means without pity; weeping with pity and giving light sentences is the opposite.

visual.alt: A shark beside a block of ice, suggesting a cold, hard hunter.

words.frame: A ruthless person will ___ to get ___.

words.def: The act of making up for past wrongs so that you earn forgiveness or a fresh start.
words.ex: The novel traces the thief's long road to redemption, as he repays the people he robbed.
words.ex2: The coach offered the player a chance at redemption by letting him take the last shot.
words.nonExample: Repeating the same harmful act and feeling nothing is not a path to redemption.

apps.academic: Redemption is a common theme in literature, from stories of cheaters who earn forgiveness to villains who change.
apps.spoken: He got his redemption in the final game.
apps.writing: Show redemption through actions that repair harm, not only through apologies.

cloze.s: After betraying his team, Jonah worked all season to earn ___ by staying late and helping others improve.

cloze2.s: In the play's last act, the cruel king finds ___ by giving up his crown to protect his people.

misuse.s: The villain's redemption was complete when he caused even more harm and felt no regret.
misuse.why: Redemption means making up for past wrongs; causing more harm without regret does the opposite.

visual.alt: A sunrise beside two people shaking hands.

words.frame: A character might find redemption by ___.

passage.title: Who Changes in The Salt Garden?
paras: In the novel The Salt Garden, a girl named Wren inherits a failing orchard from an aunt she barely knew. Readers praise the plot, but the real strength of the book is its characters. Wren is a dynamic character: the villagers around her stay much the same, while she changes in ways the story lets us watch.

At the start, Wren is idealistic. She believes that honesty and hard work will save the orchard, and she refuses every shortcut. Her neighbor, Mr. Calder, is pragmatic. He cares only about what works, and he will trade fruit, land, or favors with anyone who can pay. Their arguments drive the book, and neither of them is entirely wrong.

The antagonist is Marguerite Voss, a developer who wants the land. She is ruthless: she quietly buys up the orchard's debts so that Wren cannot pay them, and she smiles while she does it. Because Voss opposes Wren's goal at every turn, she makes the stakes clear.

Two other characters complicate the picture. Silas, the old gardener, is enigmatic. He answers every question with another question, and we never learn where he came from. Mr. Calder is also volatile, calm one moment and shouting the next, so we cannot predict whether he will help Wren or harm her.

The turning point comes after Voss ruins the first harvest. Wren becomes disillusioned, and she stops believing that honesty matters. Then, in midwinter, she finds Silas's old account book and has an epiphany: the orchard has survived for forty years because neighbors traded small favors, not because anyone worked alone. The sudden understanding changes what she wants.

The book ends with a quiet act of redemption. Mr. Calder, who earlier betrayed Wren, testifies against Voss and loses a valuable contract. The author refuses to make this simple or complete. It is a single costly choice, not an erasing of his past. That, to me, is what makes these characters feel real.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the phrase “a dynamic character” describes a character who
choices: is full of loud energy in every scene
changes in important ways during the story
never speaks to the other characters
opposes the main character's goal
qs.why: The writer explains that the villagers stay much the same while Wren changes in ways the story lets us watch.

qs.q: Why does the writer call Marguerite Voss the antagonist?
choices: She is the oldest character in the book.
She helps Wren with the orchard.
She is the narrator of the story.
She opposes Wren's goal of saving the orchard.
qs.why: The writer says that Voss opposes Wren's goal at every turn, which is what makes her the antagonist.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Mr. Calder is volatile?
choices: He is calm one moment and shouting the next.
He will trade fruit, land, or favors.
He testifies against Voss in the end.
He lives next door to the orchard.
qs.why: Volatile means likely to change suddenly, and the writer says we cannot predict whether he will help Wren or harm her.

qs.q: Why does Wren become disillusioned after the first harvest?
choices: Silas refuses to answer her questions.
She decides to sell the orchard to Mr. Calder.
Voss ruins the harvest, and Wren stops believing that honesty matters.
She finds out the orchard was never worth anything.
qs.why: The writer says the turning point comes after Voss ruins the first harvest, and Wren stops believing honesty matters.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the writer's central argument?
choices: The plot of the novel is too slow for most readers.
The strength of the novel lies in characters who feel real because they change, conflict, and make costly choices.
Orchards are the best setting for any novel.
A character who has an epiphany is always a villain.
qs.why: The writer says the real strength of the book is its characters and ends by saying their changes and costly choices make them feel real.

constructed.prompt: Describe an antagonist for a story set in your school. Explain what the antagonist wants and what makes the character ruthless. Use both words.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for analyzing characters and turning points in literature, including four role-and-plot terms (antagonist, dynamic, epiphany, redemption) and six adjectives that describe flawed or contradictory people. They practice supporting a claim about a character with evidence, build a word family from ideal, and read a student's analysis of an invented novel. The unit builds on irony, foil and persona earlier in the year.

notes.va.antagonist.n: The antagonist opposes the main character; the word does not mean villain. A storm, a society, or a character's own fear can be an antagonist. Ask students for an antagonist that is not a person. The opposite is protagonist.
notes.va.epiphany.n: An epiphany is a sudden understanding. It is a tier 3 literary term, but students also know the experience. Ask them to find the sentence in a text where an epiphany happens and what the character does next. Do not use the word for slow change; that is growth.
notes.va.dynamic.adj: Dynamic is a multiple-meaning word: in literature it means changing (opposite: static), and in everyday talk it can mean full of energy (shown as a second sense). Practice by choosing characters from books the class knows and deciding whether each is dynamic or static, with evidence.
notes.va.pragmatic.adj: Pragmatic means practical and realistic. It contrasts with idealistic, so teach the two as a pair. Students may think pragmatic is negative; discuss when being pragmatic is wise. Ask which would be a better partner for a school project and why.
notes.va.idealistic.adj: Idealistic is built from ideal plus -ist plus -ic. It describes high hopes, not just kindness. Contrast with cynical and with pragmatic. Ask students for an idealistic goal that might be hard to reach.
notes.va.volatile.adj: Volatile is figurative for a mood that can flip suddenly. The chemistry sense (evaporates quickly) is shown as a second sense, so students are ready for it in science. Ask students for a volatile situation in the news or in a book, and what makes it unpredictable.
notes.va.enigmatic.adj: Enigmatic means mysterious and hard to interpret. Connect to enigma (a puzzle). Students often say it means weird; push for what makes a character hard to read. Practice by giving only a character's actions and asking what readers still cannot know.
notes.va.disillusioned.adj: Disillusioned means disappointed that something is not as good or true as you believed: dis- plus illusion plus -ed. Ask what the character used to believe. Connect to cynicism: a disillusioned person may become cynical, but the two words are not synonyms.
notes.va.ruthless.adj: Ruthless means without pity. The word ruth, an old word for pity, is rarely used alone today. Ask for evidence of ruthlessness: what does the character do without regret? Contrast with strict, which can be fair.
notes.va.redemption.n: Redemption is making up for past wrongs. It is an abstract word, so use stories students know. Ask what a character must do to deserve a fresh start. Discuss whether apologies are enough or whether actions are needed.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “Wren starts out idealistic and ends up understanding the orchard differently. That is a change, so I would call her dynamic. The writer calls Voss the antagonist because she opposes Wren's goal. I want to prove ruthless with evidence: she quietly buys the debts and smiles. That is an action that shows no pity.”
discuss: Which is more interesting in a story, a dynamic character or a character who never changes?
Is it fair to call someone enigmatic when we simply do not know them well?
Can a ruthless person experience redemption? What would it take?
misconceptions: An antagonist is always a villain.
An epiphany is a long process of change.
extend: Write a one-page analysis of a character from a book the class has read, using at least four words from the unit and two pieces of evidence.
Create a character web that shows how a protagonist, an antagonist and a foil relate to each other.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to irony, foil, persona and conform when students compare characters across a text. Revisit the pairs pragmatic and idealistic, and volatile and enigmatic after two days with new characters, and apply redemption and epiphany in the final consequences unit when discussing turning points in nonfiction.

The novel The Salt Garden, its characters and plot are invented for this passage and are not presented as a real book.
Morphology: ruthless is segmented as ruth (an old word for pity) plus -less; confirm against an etymology source. Disillusioned is segmented as dis- plus illusion plus -ed.
Sense boundaries: dynamic taught as a literary term with the energetic sense as a second sense; volatile taught in the figurative sense with the chemical sense as a second sense.
Example about Scrooge assumes Dickens's A Christmas Carol: Scrooge begins as a miser and ends generous (confirm).
